# Finding material and reusing actions {#sec-efficient-work}

A keyboard language becomes most useful when it can describe musical
relationships rather than only screen positions. Search locates notes by
properties; marks remember places; registers retain material; repeat and
macros retain actions. Each reduces a different kind of repetition.

## Finding a pitch class

A **find** seeks the next or previous note of a pitch class in any octave.
`fE` finds the next E, while `FE` finds the previous one. A following `#`
or `b` specifies a sharp or flat. `;` repeats the last find in its original
direction, and Alt-; repeats it in the opposite direction.

This suits a musical landmark such as the next bass root, without needing
to know its bar or octave. A count chooses a later occurrence. After an
operator, a find can describe the range through that landmark, so `dfE`
takes the events through the next E.

The accidental can complete a find after its letter. After an operator,
Modal revises the edit to the sharpened or flattened target as one change;
Escape at that point undoes it. The message and highlights show the target
being used, which is particularly helpful for ambiguous letter sequences.

## Searching by musical properties

`/` opens a search query. Its terms are conditions on events, not ordinary
text to find in the song title. Combined terms must all match.

| Query | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `/C4` | The exact pitch C4 |
| `/36` | MIDI note 36 |
| `/snare` | Notes on a named snare pitch from this track's drum map |
| `/C` | C in any octave |
| `/A3-A5` | Pitches in that range |
| `/vel<60` | Notes with attack velocity below 60 |
| `/C4 vel<60` | Quiet C4 notes |
| `/len<1/16` | Notes shorter than a sixteenth |
| `/cc64>63` | Sustain-controller values above 63 |
| `/bend` | Pitch-bend events |
| `/outside D dorian` | Notes outside that key and scale |
| `/inside D dorian` | Notes inside it |

Enter accepts the query. Matches are highlighted, with the match count in
the feedback. `n` and `N` visit the next and previous matches, wrapping at
the ends.

When searching by drum name, enter the name on its own. A short name such
as `/snare` can match several articulations. Each choice shows the full name,
MIDI number and the number of notes on that pitch in the current track. The
most-used pitches come first. Use Tab or the arrow keys to choose one, then
press Enter. The usual search keys then move between hits on that pitch.

`*` and `#` start a search for the exact pitch under the cursor,
forwards or backwards, without typing a `/` query.

`/` followed by Enter with an empty query, `:noh`, or `, S c` clears the search.

The search concerns the current track in this edition. It does not silently
turn into a search across every arrangement track.

## Search and selection are different

Highlighting identifies matches; it does not automatically make them the
target of every edit. This distinction allows a passage to be inspected
without turning a later ordinary edit into a global replacement.

The `, S` selection group connects the two when desired. Lower-case `b`,
`s`, `t` and `v` select a bar, section, track or the visible material.
Their upper-case equivalents select only the search matches within that
scope. For example, `, S T` selects the matches on the track. In Visual
mode, `, S m` keeps only matching events in the existing selection.

The `gn` object means the match at the cursor, or the next one. An operator
with it changes that match and advances to the next. This creates a
controlled review pattern: `.` applies the same change to the next match,
while `n` skips it. The decision remains local at each occurrence, rather
than requiring one all-or-nothing change across every match.

A filter transform deletes matches. Searching, selecting matches and deleting
matches are therefore three separate intentions, with increasingly broad
consequences.

## Marks and labels

A **mark** is a place named by a letter: `ma` records mark a and `'a`
returns to it. The letter is chosen for the task, such as a place being
compared with the current passage. Marks are saved with the song and move
with their sections.

Every lower-case letter from `a` to `z` can name a mark. Marks, named
registers and macros have separate sets of names: mark a, register a and
macro a can all exist independently. Setting one does not overwrite either
of the others.

`''` returns to the place before the last jump. `, l m` (`:marks`) lists
marks and `, l x` deletes them, asking which letters (`:mark-delete a`, or
`a-d` for several). A mark can also end an operator range, as in
`d'a`. The same navigation destination can therefore describe music to
act on.

A label has a full name and can describe the piece to a reader; a mark is
a compact working bookmark. Neither has to create a new section. The
palette's apostrophe prefix finds labels and marks by name.

## Going back: the jump list

Checking something elsewhere is common: the bass line in the chorus, the
tempo at the bridge, a phrase in another song. Getting back to where you were
working shouldn't need a mark set in advance. Modal keeps a **jump list**,
like a web browser's history: `Ctrl-o` goes back to where the last jump came
from, and again to the one before, and `Ctrl-i` goes forward again. Think of
**o** as *out*, back the way you came, and **i** as *in*, as Vim has them.

A jump is a move that leaves the neighbourhood rather than stepping through
it: `gg` and `G`, the section and label motions, going to a mark, a search,
the palette's go-to, and stopping playback in place. Changing view counts
too, as does Backspace, and so does switching to another open song. Moving
a note, a beat or a bar at a time doesn't, so the list keeps the places that
matter rather than every step.

For example, editing a fill in bar 23 of the piano roll, you jump with `ga`
to the arrangement and `G` to the end to see how the song closes, then
switch to another song with `]f` to compare it. Three presses of `Ctrl-o`
bring you back: into the first song at the arrangement's end, to bar 23 where
the arrangement opened, and to the fill in the piano roll. `Ctrl-i` retraces
them. A count goes several places at once: `3 Ctrl-o`.

As in a browser, going back and then jumping somewhere new forgets the places
you had stepped back over. The list holds the last hundred places for the
session; a place in a song that has been closed is dropped. `:jumps` lists
the places, oldest first, with `>` beside the one you last went to.

`''` is still the quickest way to swap between two places: it goes to where
the last jump came from, and again straight back. Use `''` to compare two
places and `Ctrl-o` to retrace a longer path.

## Registers keep material

The unnamed register holds recently yanked or deleted material. A **named
register** keeps a copy deliberately: `"a` before a yank, delete or put
chooses register a. An upper-case name appends to it, so `"A` adds material
to register a instead of replacing it. `:registers` shows the stored contents.

The full set `a` to `z` is available for named registers, separate from
marks and macros. Upper-case letters append to the corresponding lower-case
register; they do not name another set of 26 registers.

For example, `"ayib` yanks the current bar into a; `"ap` later puts from a.
Another delete can use the unnamed register without losing that named copy.
Registers can retain different kinds of material, including events, sections
and whole tracks, but a put must still use a context appropriate to its kind.

These registers are internal to Modal and shared by every open song, so
material yanked in one song can be put in another (see @sec-files). System
clipboard exchange is not part of this edition. Named copies should not be
treated as substitutes for saving a song.

## Repeating an edit

`.` repeats the last change, including its target and answers. The target
is reinterpreted at the new cursor location: a change to a bar can be applied
to another bar without specifying its parameters again. A count before the
repeat substitutes for the recorded count.

Undo (`u`) and redo (Ctrl-R) restore the edit and its editing location. Some
continuous gestures, such as repeated moves of the same selected notes,
are grouped into one step. This makes undo reflect the musical gesture
rather than every key repeat.

Repeat is most useful when the intended edit is already correct. A Visual
selection or a search-match workflow can be preferable when the target still
needs to be inspected before each change.

## Macros keep sequences of actions

A **macro** records keys rather than musical events. `Qa` starts recording
into macro a, and `Q` ends it. `@a` plays it; `@@` repeats the last macro,
and a count such as `3@a` plays it three times. Upper-case `QA` appends to a.
`:macros` lists the recordings.

Macro names also run from `a` to `z`, independently of marks and registers.
`Qz` records macro z and `@z` plays it. The upper-case recording form appends
to its lower-case macro, rather than selecting a separate macro name.

A macro is suited to a repeated editing procedure with several actions,
where `.` would remember only the most recent change. Because it records
keys, its effect depends on the starting view, cursor, settings and musical
context. A sequence intended for a piano-roll note is not made independent
of context by recording it.

Modal stops a macro when a command is refused, rather than carrying on from
an unexpected state. A warning that accompanies a successful operation does
not itself mean refusal. Macros are remembered between sessions in the
machine's state files; they are not embedded in every song.

The useful progression is from a clear edit, to repeat, to a deliberate
sequence. A macro is easier to trust when its component actions and targets
are understood first.
